distinctions.note: Doleful suggests a gloomy, down-hearted look or sound, while dolorous suggests deeper, more solemn grief.
Sorrowful is more common and neutral, whereas dolorous is more formal and literary.

examples.everyday: He gave a dolorous sigh when the game was rained out again.
examples.professional: The report had a dolorous tone that made the whole team feel worse about the failed quarter.
examples.analytical: The poet's dolorous language transforms personal grief into a meditation on mortality.

nuance.analogy: A dolorous mood is like a heavy gray cloud that refuses to move and blocks out the sun.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dolor, meaning pain or grief.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'dolerous' or 'doleful' in spelling
Using it in casual speech where 'sad' is more natural

dolorous.etymology: From Middle English *dolorous*, from Old French *dolerous* (modern French *douloureux*), from Late Latin *dolōrōsus* (“painful”), from Latin *dolor*.

senses.definition: A scalar product.

core.definition: A single number computed from two vectors by multiplying their matching components and adding the results.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on "PRAH" in "product," and "dot" is weakly stressed. The vowel in "dot" is the same as in "hot" in General American. The "t" in "product" is aspirated and clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "dot product" in linear algebra, physics, machine learning, and computer graphics. In textbooks it may also be called the scalar product or inner product. In a meeting, a data scientist might say "the dot product of the two embeddings" to refer to a similarity calculation.

distinctions.note: The dot product gives a scalar, while the cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both inputs and exists only in three dimensions.
A matrix product is a general operation on matrices, while the dot product is specifically for two vectors and returns one number.

examples.everyday: My physics homework asked us to find the dot product of two force vectors, so I had to multiply the matching parts and add them.
examples.professional: We use the dot product of the query and document embeddings as a fast similarity score in the search index.
examples.analytical: The dot product is bilinear and symmetric, and its value equals the product of the magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between the vectors.

nuance.analogy: The dot product is like measuring how much two arrows point in the same direction, returning one number that rises when they align.
nuance.etymology: "Dot" refers to the dot symbol used in the notation, and "product" comes from Latin productus, "brought forth."
common_mistakes: Saying "dot product" as one word or with the stress on "dot."
Confusing it with the cross product, which gives a vector rather than a number.

dot-product.etymology: In reference to the symbol · used to denote the operation.

senses.definition: One who requires proof before believing.
One who finds belief difficult. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: A person who refuses to believe something until they have clear proof, often used playfully or critically.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'DOWT' and on 'TAH', and the 'Thomas' ending is a reduced 'muss'. In General American the vowel in 'Thomas' matches the cot vowel, so it sounds like 'TAH'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative, though often said playfully about a friend who needs evidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when someone insists on seeing proof, as in 'Don't be a doubting Thomas, I really did fix it.' It is usually lighthearted among friends and coworkers. In religious settings it is a reference to the apostle, so it may sound pointed when used about a person's faith.

distinctions.note: A skeptic habitually questions claims, while a doubting Thomas specifically wants physical or direct proof before believing.
A cynic assumes the worst about people's motives, while a doubting Thomas simply wants evidence.

examples.everyday: Don't be a doubting Thomas, I really did pick up the dry cleaning this time.
examples.professional: Our CFO is a doubting Thomas about forecast models until she sees the backtests on real data.
examples.analytical: Thomas's demand to see the wounds before believing has become a model for insisting on evidence without rejecting faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a customer who will not trust the store's new price until he sees it on the receipt in his own hand.
nuance.etymology: Named for the apostle Thomas in John 20; Thomas comes from Aramaic t'oma, meaning twin.
common_mistakes: Writing 'doubting thomas' in lowercase in formal writing; the name is usually capitalized.
Using it to mean someone who doubts only in general, without the idea of demanding proof.
nuance.biblical_note: In John 20:24-29 the apostle Thomas, called Didymus, says he will not believe that Jesus has risen until he sees the nail marks and touches them. Jesus later appears to the group, including Thomas, and invites him to touch the wounds. Thomas answers with the confession 'My Lord and my God!' The Greek name Didymos means twin.

doubting-thomas.etymology: Originates from the story of the Apostle Thomas in the Gospel of John, where he refuses to believe that Jesus has risen from the dead unless he can see and touch the wounds of Jesus himself.

senses.definition: Exhibiting duality.
Being the space of all linear functionals of (some other space).
Being the dual of some other category; containing the same objects but with source and target reversed for all morphisms.
Characterized by having two (usually equivalent) components.
senses.example: a dual-motor vehicle

senses.definition: Pertaining to two, pertaining to a pair of.
senses.example: dual engine failure

senses.definition: Pertaining to a grammatical number in certain languages that refers to two of something, such as a pair of shoes.
senses.example: Modern Arabic displays a dual number, as did Homeric Greek.

senses.definition: Of a regular polyhedron with V vertices and F faces, the regular polyhedron having F vertices and V faces.
senses.example: The octahedron is the dual of the cube. The icosahedron is the dual of the dodecahedron.

senses.definition: Of a vector in an inner product space, the linear functional corresponding to taking the inner product with that vector. The set of all duals is a vector space called the dual space.
Of an item that is one of a pair, the other item in the pair.
The dual number.
A head-to-head match or meet between two teams, such as two high schools or colleges.
To convert from single to dual; specifically, to convert a single-carriageway road to a dual carriageway.

core.definition: Having two parts, aspects, or functions; combining two things of the same kind, such as a dual-core processor or dual citizenship.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say 'DOO-ul', with no y sound; the stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a light 'ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, descriptive and precise.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people more often say 'two' or 'double', but 'dual' is common in technical contexts like 'dual monitors' or 'dual citizenship'. It sounds formal in casual conversation. In mathematics, it has specialized meanings like 'dual space'.

distinctions.note: Double is the everyday word for two of something; dual is more formal or technical and emphasizes two distinct functions or aspects.
Twin refers to two similar or paired things, often identical in form; dual stresses two roles or functions within one thing.

examples.everyday: My sister has dual citizenship, so she carries both passports when she travels.
examples.professional: Our new laptop has dual monitor outputs, which makes it easier to run the dashboard and the notebook side by side.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the text has a dual purpose: it is both a historical record and a theological argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin with two faces, each side different but part of the same object.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'dualis', from 'duo' (two).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a y sound, like 'JOO-ul'.
Using 'dual' in casual speech where 'two' or 'double' sounds more natural.

dual.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *dualis* (“two”), from *duo* (“two”) + adjective suffix *-alis*.

senses.definition: A period of time in which a system or component remains in a given state.
A brief pause in the motion of part of a mechanism to allow an operation to be completed.
A planned delay in a timed control program.

In a petrol engine, the period of time the ignition points are closed to let current flow through the ignition coil in between each spark. This is measured as an angle in degrees around the camshaft in the distributor which controls the points, for example in a 4-cylinder engine it might be 55° (spark at 90° intervals, points closed for 55° between each).
To live; to reside.
To linger (on); to remain fixated. [with on ‘a particular thought, idea, etc.’]
senses.example: Stop dwelling on the past!

senses.definition: To be in a given state.
To abide; to remain; to continue.

core.definition: To keep thinking or talking about something for a long time, or to live in a place. The everyday sense is to linger on a thought or worry.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short e, like 'bell'. Do not add a vowel after the d, and do not say 'dwell-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when used with 'on', because it suggests spending too much mental energy on something. Neutral when it means to live somewhere, which sounds formal or literary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'don't dwell on it' or 'she dwelled on her mistakes' in casual talk, usually to mean you should stop worrying about something. The sense 'to live in a place' sounds biblical, poetic or formal, so in everyday speech Americans say 'live' instead. A natural reply to someone who keeps worrying is 'Yeah, I know, but let's move on.'

distinctions.note: 'Live' is the ordinary everyday word for where you reside, while 'dwell' sounds formal or literary.
'Linger' suggests staying somewhere a little longer than needed, while 'dwell' usually refers to staying in your mind on a topic, often too long.
'Ponder' means to think carefully and deliberately about something, while 'dwell' often suggests unhealthy or repetitive focus.

collocations: dwell in the house of the Lord

examples.everyday: Don't dwell on the bad review; most people loved the show.
examples.professional: We shouldn't dwell on last quarter's delays; let's focus on the fix for next sprint.
examples.analytical: The author dwells on the inner conflict of the protagonist rather than on the external plot.

nuance.analogy: Like a song stuck in your head, a thought you dwell on keeps playing again and again.
nuance.etymology: From Old English dwellan, meaning 'to lead astray or delay', later 'to remain'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'dwell at home' or 'dwell in Boston' in casual speech, where 'live' is more natural.
Pronouncing it with a long vowel, as in 'dwail'.
Using 'dwell' for a short visit or passing thought, when 'think about' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, 'dwell' often means to live in the presence of God or to have God's presence among people. The Hebrew shakhan means 'to dwell or settle', and the Greek skenoo means 'to tabernacle' or pitch a tent. Psalm 23:6 speaks of dwelling in the house of the LORD forever. John 1:14 says the Word dwelt among us. Psalm 91:1 describes the one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High.

senses.definition: Great energy, drive, force, or power; vigor of body, mind, or personality; oomph or pizzazz.
Dynamic reality; active energy; continuous change, progress, or activity.
senses.example: The fact that the war is no longer the main issue in the election points to the dynamism of foreign affairs.

senses.definition: Any of several philosophical theories that attempt to explain the universe by an immanent force.

core.definition: Great energy, drive and readiness for change and action, especially in a person, team or organization.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'DY'. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, 'nuh', and the final syllable is a weak 'um'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises energy, initiative and momentum.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dynamism' in business writing, reviews and speeches to praise an organization's energy, as in 'the company's dynamism attracted investors'. In everyday talk people would say 'energy', 'drive' or 'a lot of go-getter spirit'. It can sound a little stiff in casual speech, so use it in writing or formal presentations.

distinctions.note: 'Energy' is the everyday word for vitality, while 'dynamism' is more formal and suggests a continuous, forward-moving force.
'Drive' suggests ambition and determination, while 'dynamism' emphasizes vigor and capacity for change.

examples.everyday: My grandmother has a lot of dynamism for her age; she still goes hiking every morning.
examples.professional: The new director brought real dynamism to the sales team, and our numbers rose within a quarter.
examples.analytical: Hegel's account of history emphasizes a dynamism in which contradictions drive the development of ideas.

nuance.analogy: Dynamism is like a river in spring, full of force and always moving forward.
nuance.etymology: From 'dynamic', from Greek dynamis, 'power' or 'force', plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'dynamism' with 'dynamics' when talking about group interactions.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, 'dy-NAM-iz-um'.
Using 'dynamism' for physical strength alone when 'vigor' or 'energy' is more natural.

dynamism.etymology: From English *dynamic* (or directly from Ancient Greek *δύναμις* (“power”)) + *ism*.

senses.definition: Intense pleasure.
A state of emotion so intense that a person is carried beyond rational thought and self-control.
senses.example: an ecstasy of remorse

senses.definition: A trance, frenzy, or rapture associated with mystic or prophetic exaltation.
The drug MDMA, a synthetic entactogen of the methylenedioxyphenethylamine family, especially in a tablet form.
(dated) A state in which sensibility, voluntary motion, and (largely) mental power are suspended, and the body is erect and inflexible.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To experience intense pleasure.
To cause intense pleasure in.

core.definition: Intense, overwhelming joy or pleasure; a feeling of being carried away by emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The "-sy" ending sounds like "see", and the middle vowel is a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing joy or spiritual rapture. In American English it can also refer to the drug MDMA, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ecstasy for very strong happiness, usually in writing or in dramatic speech, as in "pure ecstasy" or "in ecstasy." In everyday talk, "ecstatic" is more common. In contemporary American speech, "ecstasy" often refers to the club drug, so avoid it in casual joking unless you mean that.

distinctions.note: Happiness is a general, calm state of contentment; ecstasy is an intense, overwhelming peak of joy.
Joy is deep gladness; ecstasy suggests a stronger feeling that takes you out of ordinary awareness.

examples.everyday: She danced with pure ecstasy when she heard the band play her favorite song.
examples.professional: The team was in ecstasy when the model finally passed every test in the release.
examples.analytical: Mystics have long described ecstasy as a movement of the soul beyond ordinary thought.

nuance.analogy: Ecstasy is like a wave that lifts you off your feet, sweeping you past your usual awareness.
nuance.etymology: From Greek ekstasis, "standing outside oneself", from ek- "out" and histanai "to stand".
common_mistakes: Using "ecstasy" in casual talk where a listener may think of the drug; "ecstatic" is safer.
Saying "I am ecstasy" instead of "I am ecstatic".
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament the Greek word ekstasis, meaning a state of being outside one's normal mind, appears in Acts 10:10 and Acts 11:5, where Peter falls into a trance and sees a vision. In Mark 5:42 the same Greek root describes the amazement of the onlookers when a girl is restored to life. The Septuagint also uses ekstasis for the deep sleep that fell on Adam in Genesis 2:21.

ecstasy.etymology: From Old French *estaise* (“ecstasy, rapture”), from Latin *ecstasis*, from Ancient Greek *ἔκστασις*, from *ἐξίστημι* (“to displace”), from *ἐκ* (“out”) and *ἵστημι* (“to stand”).

core.definition: In the Bible, the eldest son of Jesse and older brother of David, who scorned David when he came to the battle with Goliath.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EL. The middle syllable is a short 'ee' and the final syllable rhymes with 'cab'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a name; in Bible study it often suggests jealousy or pride.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say EL-ee-ab, with the final syllable like 'cab'. It is used mostly in Bible study, sermons and religious writing, and is also a rare given name in the United States.

distinctions.note: Eli is the priest at Shiloh who raised Samuel. Eliab is David's older brother, a soldier in Saul's army.
Eliakim was a royal steward under King Hezekiah. Eliab is David's brother from the time of Saul.

examples.everyday: In Sunday school we talked about how David's brother Eliab got angry at him for coming to the battle.
examples.professional: When teaching the story of David, I point out that Eliab's reaction shows how easily people misjudge a younger sibling's calling.
examples.analytical: Eliab's rebuke in 1 Samuel 17 reveals a tension between family expectations and God's choice of David as king.

nuance.analogy: Like an older sibling who assumes the family's future belongs to him, only to be surprised when the younger one is chosen.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ʾĕlîʾāb, meaning God is father, from ʾēl, God, and ʾāb, father.
common_mistakes: Confusing Eliab with Eli, the priest, because the names sound alike.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew ʾĕlîʾāb, 'God is father'. In 1 Samuel 16:6–7 Samuel looks at Eliab and assumes he is the chosen king, but God tells him that people look at outward appearance while God looks at the heart. In 1 Samuel 17:28 Eliab angrily rebukes David for coming to the battlefield and accuses him of pride. In 1 Chronicles 2:13 Eliab appears in the genealogy as one of Jesse's sons.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an ellipse.
Of or pertaining to a broad field of mathematics that originates from the problem of calculating arc lengths of an ellipse.
senses.example: elliptic integral

senses.definition: That has coefficients satisfying a condition analogous to the condition for the general equation for a conic section to be of an ellipse.
senses.example: elliptic partial differential equation

senses.definition: Of, or showing ellipsis; having a word or words omitted; elliptical.
Oval, with a short or no point.
An elliptical function, equation, path, etc.

core.definition: Relating to an ellipse, or in mathematics, a branch of study involving curves and functions defined by elliptic integrals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LIP. The final syllable is short -tik, not -teek. Do not pronounce the t as a flap, because it is a clear t here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in mathematics and physics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elliptic almost only in mathematics and science classrooms or research. In most cases, elliptical is the more common everyday adjective, as in elliptical trainer or elliptical orbit. Elliptic is often used in phrases like elliptic curve or elliptic function.

distinctions.note: Elliptic is preferred in technical names such as elliptic curve. Elliptical is used more in everyday and general descriptions, like an elliptical orbit or gym machine.

examples.everyday: My cryptography class spends a week on elliptic curves, which is harder than I expected.
examples.professional: Our security team uses elliptic curve cryptography for the new key exchange because it offers strong protection with smaller keys.
examples.analytical: The elliptic integrals studied by Legendre and Jacobi provided the foundation for a broad theory of elliptic functions.

nuance.analogy: An elliptic curve is like a stretched circle with a special rule for points, which turns out to be very useful for secure codes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek elleipsis, a falling short or omission, via the ellipse.
common_mistakes: Using elliptic and elliptical interchangeably in all contexts, even when elliptic curve is the fixed term.
Stressing the first syllable as EL-ip-tik.

elliptic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ἐλλειπτικός*, from *ἐλλείπω* (“I leave out, omit”).

senses.definition: Decorated with embroidery; covered in decorative needlework.
Embellished; elaborate, especially when containing superfluous or fictitious details.

core.definition: Decorated with embroidery, meaning stitched designs on fabric; also describing a story with added, exaggerated details.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, BROY, and the final -ered is one reduced syllable sounding like 'erd', not 'ared'. The r in 'embr' is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing fabric or clothing; slightly negative when describing a story, meaning exaggerated or made up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use embroidered for a shirt, pillow, or tablecloth with stitched designs, often with a monogram or logo. For stories, it suggests someone added details to make an account more interesting, often in a mildly critical way, as in 'His embroidered tale of the fishing trip grew larger each time.'

distinctions.note: Decorated is a broad word for anything made more attractive; embroidered specifically means decorated with needlework.
Exaggerated describes overstating facts in general, while embroidered in the figurative sense stresses added invented details.

examples.everyday: My grandmother gave me a pillow with embroidered flowers on it.
examples.professional: The uniform shop can add an embroidered company logo to every polo shirt.
examples.analytical: The memoir is embroidered with invented scenes that undermine its claim to historical accuracy.

nuance.analogy: Like a plain cloth with thread stitched on top, an embroidered account is a simple story with extra decoration added.
nuance.etymology: From embroider, from Middle French embroder, to ornament with needlework.
common_mistakes: Saying 'embroidered' as if it has two syllables in the middle; the word is three syllables before the ending: im-BROY-derd.
Using embroidered only for stories; in everyday American English it most often describes fabric.

senses.definition: A technique in poetry whereby a sentence is carried over to the next line without pause.

core.definition: In poetry, the continuation of a sentence or phrase from one line to the next without a pause at the end of the line.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on JAM, the second syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'ment'. Pronounce the 'j' as in 'judge' and don't stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a neutral technical term from literary criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enjambment in poetry classes, literary criticism and discussions of poems. It is not used in everyday conversation, so you would only hear it in classrooms, reviews or literary discussion. A common reply in a class might be 'Yes, the enjambment creates tension because the reader has to keep going.'

distinctions.note: A caesura is a pause within a line, while enjambment is the lack of a pause at the end of a line.
An end-stop is a line that finishes with punctuation or a natural pause, the opposite of enjambment.

examples.everyday: My sister is taking a poetry class and keeps talking about enjambment, so I asked her to explain it.
examples.professional: For the grant report, we discussed how the poet's enjambment mirrors the sense of uncertainty in the text.
examples.analytical: Milton's enjambment in Paradise Lost forces the reader to carry the sentence across the line, enacting the movement of the argument itself.

nuance.analogy: Enjambment is like a conversation that keeps going without a breath, so the listener is pulled into the next line.
nuance.etymology: From French enjamber ('to stride over'), from en- and jambe ('leg').
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in EN-jam-ment.
Pronouncing the 'j' as 'y' or using a hard 'g' sound.

senses.definition: A logical fallacy resulting from the use of multiple meanings of a single expression.
The use of expressions susceptible of a double signification, possibly intentionally and with the aim of misleading.

core.definition: Deliberately vague or misleading wording, or a logical fallacy where one word has two different meanings in an argument.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAY, the fourth syllable. The -tion ending is a 'shun' sound, not 'tee-on.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests dishonest evasion or a flaw in reasoning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'equivocation' in political commentary, legal discussion, and philosophy. In logic classes, it names a specific fallacy. In everyday talk people more often say 'dodging' or 'spin.' Calling someone's answer 'an equivocation' is direct and can sound confrontational.

distinctions.note: 'Ambiguity' is a neutral property of language; 'equivocation' describes deliberate or fallacious use of multiple meanings.
'Evasion' is broader and covers any avoidance; 'equivocation' specifically involves wording that is technically true but misleading.

examples.everyday: Her answer about the budget was pure equivocation, so I still don't know if the project is funded.
examples.professional: The memo's claim about 'user data' is an equivocation, since the team used it to mean both raw logs and anonymized records.
examples.analytical: The argument fails because of an equivocation on the word 'cause,' which shifts from physical causation to explanatory reasons.

nuance.analogy: Like a magician using the same card name for two different cards, misleading the audience without technically lying.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin aequivocatio, from aequivocare 'to call by the same name.'
common_mistakes: Using 'equivocation' as a synonym for 'equivalence' or 'equality.'
Confusing the noun with the verb 'equivocate' in sentences.

senses.definition: The state of being a hermit; seclusion from society.

core.definition: The way of life or condition of living as a hermit, withdrawn from ordinary society.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ending '-ism' is pronounced 'iz-um' with a reduced final vowel. Keep the middle vowels short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a religious or philosophical practice without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in historical, religious, or scholarly contexts. In ordinary talk, people say 'living as a hermit' or 'living alone in seclusion'. It is not used for simple loneliness.

distinctions.note: 'Asceticism' is broader and refers to strict self-discipline and denial of comforts, while 'eremitism' specifically refers to living alone.
'Monasticism' refers to community religious life, while 'eremitism' refers to solitary life.

examples.everyday: My aunt talks about eremitism like it is a dream, but she only wants a quiet weekend away from her kids.
examples.professional: Our church history course spends two weeks on the rise of eremitism in the fourth century.
examples.analytical: Eremitism raised a theological question: can a person find holiness by withdrawing from the community that the gospel commands them to serve?

nuance.analogy: Eremitism is like taking a long walk alone to think, but pushed to a whole life.
nuance.etymology: From eremite, from Greek erēmos, 'desert, solitary', with the suffix '-ism'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for loneliness; it describes a chosen way of life.
Stressing the last syllable.

senses.definition: A system of doctrines concerning final matters, such as death.
The study of the end times—the end of the world, notably in Christian and Islamic theology, the second coming of Christ, the Apocalypse, or the Last Judgment.

core.definition: The branch of theology that studies the last things: death, judgment, the end of the age, and the final destiny of humanity and the world.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on 'TAH', the third syllable. The 'ch' is a /k/ sound, not 'ch'. Many Americans pronounce the stressed vowel as 'ah' due to the cot-caught merger, and the last part is 'luh-jee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly. It describes a field of study, though end-times topics can carry strong emotion in popular religion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'eschatology' mainly in seminaries, theology classes, and religious studies. In popular American Christianity, the same topic appears as 'end times' or 'prophecy'. Theologians distinguish 'realized eschatology' (the end already begun) from 'future eschatology'. The word is also used loosely for any view of ultimate destiny.

distinctions.note: Apocalyptic is a literary and theological style with visions of cosmic upheaval; eschatology is the broader doctrine of last things.
Soteriology is the doctrine of salvation; eschatology is the doctrine of final events and destiny.
End times is the popular term for the future period before the end, while eschatology is the academic study.

examples.everyday: I'm taking a class on eschatology, which is basically what the Bible says about the end of all things.
examples.professional: This semester's seminar will survey major views of eschatology, from premillennialism to amillennialism.
examples.analytical: Jesus's teaching is often read through the lens of inaugurated eschatology, in which the age to come has already broken into the present without yet being fully realized.

nuance.analogy: Like reading the last chapter of a story to understand what the whole plot has been heading toward.
nuance.etymology: From Greek eschatos, 'last,' plus -logia, 'study of'; coined in the 19th century.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ch' as in 'church' instead of /k/.
Stressing the first syllable: ES-kuh-tol-uh-jee.
Confusing it with 'scatology', which is a different word entirely.
nuance.biblical_note: The word comes from Greek eschatos ('last') and refers to biblical teaching about the last days. Daniel 12:2 speaks of many who sleep in the dust awakening to everlasting life or contempt. 1 Corinthians 15:51-57 describes the resurrection of the dead and the final victory over death. Revelation 21:1-4 envisions a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with his people.

traditions.view: Orthodoxy affirms Christ's second coming, the resurrection of the dead, and the Last Judgment, with the Church already participating in the age to come through the liturgy. It generally avoids detailed timelines and does not teach purgatory.

Catholic teaching includes particular judgment at death, heaven, hell, and purgatory, followed by Christ's return, the general resurrection, and the Last Judgment. Detailed predictions of dates are discouraged.

Protestants affirm Christ's return, resurrection, and judgment but differ on details: premillennialists, amillennialists, and postmillennialists disagree on the millennium, and dispensationalists teach a rapture. Most reject purgatory.

senses.definition: A philosophical notion, or system of ethics, which measures happiness in relation to morality.

core.definition: An ethical theory that holds happiness, understood as flourishing, is the highest good and is closely tied to moral virtue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MOH, the same syllable as in 'eudaimonia', and the ending is 'iz-um' with a reduced vowel. Don't add an extra syllable at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a philosophical position without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: This is an academic term used in philosophy courses, ethics papers and debates about the nature of the good life. Americans would rarely use it outside those settings. People usually say 'Aristotelian ethics' or 'virtue ethics' when speaking casually, and 'eudaimonism' when they want to name the view precisely.

distinctions.note: Hedonism says pleasure is the highest good; eudaimonism says flourishing and virtue are.
Utilitarianism judges actions by their total happiness; eudaimonism judges by the virtue of the person acting.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor says eudaimonism is about living well, not just feeling good.
examples.professional: Her ethics paper defends a eudaimonism that connects happiness to moral character.
examples.analytical: Eudaimonism treats morality and happiness as joined, so the virtuous person is also the one who flourishes.

nuance.analogy: Eudaimonism is like a tree: the fruit of happiness depends on the roots of virtue.
nuance.etymology: From eudaimonia, from Greek eudaimōn, 'having a good spirit', plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'hedonism', which is about pleasure.
Using it for any cheerful attitude; it names a specific philosophical theory.

senses.definition: An instance of euphuism.
Misconstruction of euphemism.
(historical) An ornate style of writing (in Elizabethan England) marked by the excessive use of alliteration, antithesis and mythological similes.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: An ornate, affected style of English prose from Elizabethan England, marked by heavy alliteration, balanced antithesis and mythological comparisons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, YOO. The middle -fyoo- is a single syllable, and the ending -ism is a reduced schwa, 'um.'

nuance.connotation: Negative in modern use. It suggests showy, overwrought or insincere writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use euphuism mainly in literary history, English classes, and criticism of wordy writing. It is not a casual word. In everyday talk people would just say 'flowery' or 'over-the-top.' Be careful not to confuse it with euphemism.

distinctions.note: A euphemism is a mild word used in place of a harsh one; euphuism is an ornate style of writing.
Purple prose is any excessively ornate writing; euphuism refers to a specific Elizabethan style with set patterns.

examples.everyday: Grandma's letters were full of flowery phrases that my cousin called euphuism.
examples.professional: The editor cut the euphuism from the proposal so the executives could read it quickly.
examples.analytical: Lyly's Euphues exemplifies euphuism, where antithesis and alliteration become the substance of the argument rather than its ornament.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden trimmed into elaborate shapes: impressive to look at, but it hides the natural growth.
nuance.etymology: From Euphues, the name of the witty young man in John Lyly's 1578 novel, from Greek euphyēs 'well-grown, graceful.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'euphemism,' which means a gentle substitute for a harsh word.
Saying 'yoo-FYOO-iz-um' with the stress on the wrong syllable.

euphuism.etymology: From Euphues (Ancient Greek *ευφυής* (“graceful, witty”)) *ism*, after the titular character in John Lyly’s didactic romance Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578).

senses.definition: In an evocative manner.

core.definition: In a way that vividly brings a memory, feeling or image to mind.

pronunciation.tip: The stress stays on VAH, the second syllable, as in the adjective. The final syllable is a clear 'lee,' and the middle vowels are quick schwas.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes something done in a vivid, emotionally powerful way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evocatively mostly in writing, reviews and critical discussion of art or literature. In speech they often say 'vividly' or 'beautifully' instead. It sounds literary, so use it when describing creative work or atmosphere.

distinctions.note: 'Vividly' describes clearness of detail, while 'evocatively' emphasizes emotional or memory-bringing power.
'Beautifully' focuses on aesthetic quality, while 'evocatively' focuses on bringing something to mind.

examples.everyday: The host described the old farmhouse so evocatively that I could almost smell the apple pie.
examples.professional: The brand video portrays our product evocatively, but the call to action needs to be clearer.
examples.analytical: The essay evocatively recreates the sensory world of rural Ohio, which makes its argument about memory persuasive.

nuance.analogy: Like a painter who uses a few strokes to make you feel a whole sunset.
nuance.etymology: From evocative plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin evocare, 'to call out.'
common_mistakes: Using 'evocatively' as a synonym for 'vaguely'; it means vividly, not unclearly.
Confusing 'evocatively' with 'evocative,' using the adverb where an adjective is needed, as in 'an evocatively image.'

senses.definition: The act of heaping or piling up.
The act of exaggerating; the act of doing or representing in an excessive manner; a going beyond the bounds of truth, reason, or justice; a hyperbolical representation; hyperbole; overstatement.
senses.example: They say he's a millionnaire, but that's a massive exaggeration.

senses.definition: A representation of things beyond natural life, in expression, beauty, power, vigor.

core.definition: A statement or description that makes something seem bigger, better, or worse than it really is.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on RAY, the syllable before -shun, while the first syllable has a weaker stress. Americans say the r clearly, and the -tion ending sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It usually suggests the speaker is not telling the full truth, but it can be playful in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'That's an exaggeration' or 'No exaggeration' in ordinary conversation. 'No exaggeration' is often used to emphasize something true that sounds unbelievable. The word is common in both casual and professional speech.

distinctions.note: Hyperbole is the technical term for deliberate exaggeration as a figure of speech; exaggeration is the general everyday word.
Overstatement is more formal and common in reports and debate; exaggeration is more casual.

examples.everyday: When he said the pizza took three hours to arrive, that was a bit of an exaggeration.
examples.professional: The forecast of record traffic was a clear exaggeration, and we overprovisioned the servers.
examples.analytical: Such a reading treats the psalmist's language of cosmic collapse as literal, which is an exaggeration of the poetic intent.

nuance.analogy: An exaggeration is like a photo edited with the contrast turned all the way up: the details are still there, but the picture looks far more dramatic than the scene.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exaggeratio, from exaggerare 'to heap up', from ex- plus agger 'mound'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'exageration' by dropping the g, which is a common spelling error.
Stressing the final syllable instead of the -RAY- syllable.

senses.definition: The weighted average of outcome values, using probability as the weighting function.

core.definition: The long-run average of a random variable's possible outcomes, with each outcome weighted by its probability.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable of expected and the first of value. Say the -ed ending as a light "id" in expected, and don't pronounce the final vowel of value as a long "oo" in rushed speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in statistics, finance, data science, and decision analysis, and it appears in both classrooms and business meetings. In casual talk, people say "on average" or "the typical outcome" instead. In a meeting, saying "the expected value is about 40 dollars" sounds precise and natural.

distinctions.note: An average describes a set of observed data, while an expected value is a theoretical quantity computed from a probability distribution.
The mode is the single most probable result, but the expected value is the probability-weighted mean, which need not be a possible outcome at all.

collocations: expected value of a random variable

examples.everyday: If you bet a dollar on a coin flip that pays two dollars on heads, the expected value is a little better than zero.
examples.professional: Before we launch the A/B test, let's compare the expected value of each option so we know which one is worth the cost.
examples.analytical: The expected value of a random variable is defined as the sum, or integral, of each possible outcome multiplied by its probability, and it need not equal any outcome that can actually occur.

nuance.analogy: Think of expected value as the average of a fair-weighted lottery: each outcome counts in proportion to how likely it is.
nuance.etymology: Expect comes from Latin exspectare, "to look out for"; value comes from Latin valere, "to be strong, worth."
common_mistakes: Assuming the expected value must be a possible outcome; a die's expected value is 3.5, which cannot be rolled.
Calling it simply the average in technical writing, where the probability weighting matters.

senses.definition: In an expedient manner.

core.definition: In a way that is practical and effective for getting a result quickly, even if it is not ideal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on spee. Keep the middle syllables short and reduced, and pronounce -ly as a light "lee."

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expediently in formal writing and speech, such as reports or policy discussions. In everyday talk they would say "quickly" or "the easy way." It can imply that a choice was made to avoid a difficulty.

distinctions.note: Quickly only describes speed, while expediently suggests that the method was chosen because it was practical for the situation.
Efficiently emphasizes good use of resources, while expediently emphasizes practicality and getting past an obstacle.

examples.everyday: The mechanic fixed the leak expediently so we could still make it to the game.
examples.professional: The team resolved the outage expediently by rolling back the release instead of debugging it live.
examples.analytical: A government may act expediently in a crisis, but the long-term consequences of such action must still be weighed.

nuance.analogy: Acting expediently is like taking the nearest exit when a road is blocked: it gets you out of trouble, though it may not be the scenic route.
nuance.etymology: From expedient, from Latin expedire, "to free the feet, extricate."
common_mistakes: Using expediently to mean hurriedly or carelessly; it describes a practical choice.
Dropping the -ly ending in speech, which makes it sound like an adjective.

senses.definition: To rejoice; to be very happy, especially in triumph; to triumph (over).

core.definition: To feel or show great joy, especially after a success or a victory.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, ZULT, with a short u like in "cut." Finish with a clear t and avoid making it sound like "ex-ult" with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "exult" in writing, speeches, and news reports about triumph, such as "the crowd exulted." In everyday speech people say "celebrate" or "be thrilled." It sounds dramatic, so it suits a sports commentary or a formal toast more than a casual chat. Often followed by "in" or "over."

distinctions.note: Celebrate is the everyday word for marking a happy occasion; exult is more intense and literary, suggesting triumphant joy.
Rejoice is warmer and often religious or emotional; exult suggests a more triumphant, public joy after winning or overcoming.

examples.everyday: The fans exulted when the team scored the winning goal in the last minute.
examples.professional: Leadership exulted over the quarterly results, but we should still keep an eye on customer churn.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the hero exults in power too quickly, forgetting the cost of his victory.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner crossing the finish line with both arms raised: the joy is loud, open, and shared.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exsultare, to leap up or rejoice, from ex- (out) and saltare (to jump).
common_mistakes: Using "exult" in casual conversation where "celebrate" is more natural.
Forgetting the preposition: say "exult in victory" or "exult over the win," not just "exult the win."

exult.etymology: From Middle French *exulter*, from Latin *exsultō*, frequentative of *exsiliō* (“jump up”), from *ex-* + *saliō* (“jump, leap”).

senses.definition: Pertaining to or consisting of objective claims.
True, accurate, corresponding to reality.
Programs having content based on facts, such as documentaries.
senses.example: The BBC is increasing its budget for factual this year.

core.definition: Based on facts or actual events, and therefore true and accurate rather than opinion or imagination.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, FAK. The 'tch' sound is a 'ch' sound, and the final syllable is often reduced to 'ul' with almost no 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it signals reliability and seriousness, and it often contrasts with opinion or rumor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'factual' often in news, science, debates, and business contexts, for example 'Is that factual?' or 'That's a factual error'. In casual conversation people usually say 'true' or 'real' instead. Saying 'That's factual' alone in a relaxed conversation may sound slightly stiff.

distinctions.note: 'True' describes whether something corresponds to reality in general, while 'factual' emphasizes that the statement is based on verifiable facts rather than opinion.
'Factitious' means artificial or contrived, not based on natural facts, so it is almost the opposite in meaning.

examples.everyday: I know it sounds unbelievable, but that story is factual; my uncle was actually there.
examples.professional: Before we publish the report, we need to verify every factual claim in the executive summary.
examples.analytical: The author distinguishes between factual statements, which can be tested against evidence, and normative claims, which cannot.

nuance.analogy: A factual statement is like a measuring tape: it gives a reading you can check against the object itself.
nuance.etymology: From 'fact', from Latin 'factum', meaning 'something done'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'factual' with 'fact' as a noun in phrases like 'a factual of the matter'; the correct phrase is 'a matter of fact'.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: An irresponsible or lazy person.

core.definition: A lazy person who avoids work and responsibility, especially someone who does nothing useful despite holding a position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FAYN, and keep the second syllable short and open as 'ant'. The word is pronounced 'fayn-ANT' in French, but Americans stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes laziness or idleness, often with a note of disdain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'fainéant' in conversation; it appears mainly in historical writing, such as about the 'do-nothing kings' of the Merovingian dynasty, or in literary criticism. If you want a common alternative, say 'slacker' or 'do-nothing'. Using it in a modern workplace would sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: 'Slacker' is informal American slang for someone who avoids effort, while 'fainéant' is formal, literary, and mostly historical.
'Idler' describes someone who spends time doing nothing, often by choice, while 'fainéant' suggests someone who is nominally in charge but does nothing.

examples.everyday: My roommate is such a fainéant; he never does the dishes and then sleeps until noon.
examples.professional: The manager we inherited was a fainéant who signed off on nothing and answered no emails.
examples.analytical: Historians often describe the last Merovingian kings as fainéants, rulers who held the title while power passed to the mayors of the palace.

nuance.analogy: A fainéant is like a stage prop crown: it has the look of authority but does none of the work.
nuance.etymology: From French 'fainéant', from 'faire' (to do) with a negative sense, meaning one who does nothing.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'fay-nee-ANT' with French stress; Americans stress the first syllable.
Using it as a common everyday word; it sounds unusually formal or pretentious in casual talk.

senses.definition: Annoyed and out of patience with something that keeps happening.

core.definition: Annoyed and out of patience with something that keeps happening over and over.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'FED' and 'up' lightly, with 'with' reduced to 'with' (a short 'wih-th'). Link the words smoothly: 'FED-up-with'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, showing frustration. It is casual and common in American conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this expression to complain about something repeated, like noise, bad service, or bureaucracy. A natural reply is I hear you or Yeah, it's getting old. It is informal, so use it with friends, coworkers, and family rather than in formal letters.

distinctions.note: Fed up alone is an adjective; fed up with names the thing that frustrates you.
Sick of is slightly stronger and more informal; fed up with is common and a little more neutral.

examples.everyday: I'm fed up with the construction on my street, and it's been going on for months.
examples.professional: I'm fed up with the same bugs coming back, so let's fix the root cause this sprint.
examples.analytical: Many voters are fed up with a political system that promises reform and never delivers it.

nuance.analogy: Being fed up with something is like a dripping faucet that you have heard for weeks; eventually you can't ignore it anymore.
nuance.etymology: From feed (to supply) plus up and with; the phrase shows the sense of having been filled to the limit.
common_mistakes: Dropping with and saying I'm fed up the noise.
Using fed up with for one small annoyance; it fits better for repeated problems.

conversation.text: I'm fed up with my neighbor's dog barking all night.
She's fed up with her commute, so she's looking for a job closer to home.
We're all fed up with the rain this week.

senses.definition: To complete a form or questionnaire with requested information.
senses.example: Please fill out this application if you are interested in the job.

senses.definition: To have one's physique expand with maturity or with surplus weight.
senses.example: He began to fill out once he started college.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see fill,‎ out.

core.definition: To complete a form, application or questionnaire by writing in the information it asks for.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on "out" in this phrasal verb, while "fill" is quick and short with a dark L. Don't stretch "fill" into "feel."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a routine task, though it can feel tedious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "fill out" constantly for paperwork: doctor's office intake forms, job applications, surveys and tax forms. "Fill in" also appears, especially for blanks within a form, but "fill out" is the natural choice for completing the whole form. A typical reply is "Sure, I'll fill it out now."

distinctions.note: "Fill in" usually means writing into specific blanks, while "fill out" means completing the whole document.
"Complete" is more formal and can be used with forms, tasks or projects, while "fill out" is specific to forms and questionnaires.

examples.everyday: Can you fill out this form while I get your insurance card?
examples.professional: Please fill out the onboarding survey by Friday so HR can set up your account.
examples.analytical: Respondents who did not fill out the questionnaire completely were excluded from the analysis.

nuance.analogy: Like filling every box on a tax return until nothing is left blank.
nuance.etymology: "Fill" from Old English fyllan; "out" from Old English ut.
common_mistakes: Stressing "fill" instead of "out" in speech.
Using "fill up" for forms; "fill out" is the standard phrase for paperwork.
Saying "fill the form" without "out" in careful writing; "fill out the form" is more natural.

conversation.text: Please fill out this form and bring it back to the front desk.
I filled it out online, but I never got a confirmation.
He's filled out a lot since he started lifting weights.
I filled out the rental application online.
Do I have to fill out the paperwork every time I come?

senses.definition: The condition of being flamboyant.
A group of flamingos.

core.definition: Bold, showy style or behavior that attracts attention, such as bright clothing, dramatic gestures, or a lively personality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -BOY-. Pronounce the final -ance as a reduced 'uns', not 'ants'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive or neutral; it can praise confidence and style but may suggest excess when used critically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flamboyance' to describe performers, designers, or leaders with a bold personal style. It is common in fashion, theater, and media writing. In everyday talk people often say 'showy' or 'over the top' instead. It can sound admiring or mildly critical depending on tone.

distinctions.note: 'Ostentation' is more critical and suggests showing off wealth; 'flamboyance' suggests a bold, lively style.
'Style' is a general word for a manner of doing or looking; 'flamboyance' is more dramatic and eye-catching.

examples.everyday: I love the flamboyance of her outfits; she always stands out in a crowd.
examples.professional: The designer's flamboyance helped the brand get noticed at the trade show.
examples.analytical: The painter's flamboyance is not mere decoration; it expresses a deliberate rejection of academic restraint.

nuance.analogy: Like fireworks at a party, bright and impossible to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From flamboyant, from French flamboyer, 'to flame.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'flamingo'; a flamingo is a bird, although the words are related in origin.
Using it for quiet confidence; the word implies visible, showy display.

senses.definition: Passing quickly; of short duration.
That which flees, especially quickly; fugitive.
An automatic operation mode of an absolute signal that reserves a route for several trains following one another, without the need for dispatcher to re-set the route for each train.

core.definition: Lasting only a very short time; passing quickly and gone before you can hold onto it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The "ee" is long, and the final "-ing" is a light, reduced vowel, not a full "eeng".

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly wistful; it often describes beautiful or pleasant things that do not last.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fleeting in writing, speeches and thoughtful conversation about moments, feelings or chances. In casual speech people often say "quick" or "brief" instead. It usually collocates with abstract nouns like moment or glimpse, and it is not used for a long process.

distinctions.note: Brief is neutral and can describe any short event; fleeting adds a sense of something passing away or slipping out of reach.
Transient is more technical or academic and often describes people or things that move through a place; fleeting is more poetic and personal.

examples.everyday: I caught a fleeting glimpse of my old friend in the grocery store, but she was gone before I could say hello.
examples.professional: The window to close the deal was fleeting, so we had to decide within the hour.
examples.analytical: Fleeting experiences of transcendence, the author argues, can point beyond themselves without ever becoming a stable foundation for belief.

nuance.analogy: Like a shooting star: you see it for a second, and then it is gone.
nuance.etymology: From the verb flee in the sense of moving swiftly, with the -ing suffix.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full "eeng" instead of a light "ing".
Using fleeting for a long period of time, when the word means brief.

fleeting.etymology: From Middle English *fleten* (“to float”), from Old English *flēotan* (“to float”), from Proto-Germanic **fleutaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **plewd-*.

senses.definition: Flop per second; floating-point operation per second.

core.definition: A unit of computing speed: the number of floating-point arithmetic operations a processor can perform in one second, often written FLOPS.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one word with the stress on FLAHPS, with the short 'o' sound of 'cot'. Do not spell it out as F-L-O-P-S, since Americans say it as a word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a neutral measurement term used in computing and AI.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in computer science, hardware specifications and machine learning papers, often with a prefix such as megaflops, gigaflops, teraflops or petaflops. A single operation is called a 'flop', while the rate is 'flops' or 'FLOPS'. Outside technical contexts, you rarely hear it.

distinctions.note: FLOPs counts the total number of operations in a model or task, while FLOPS measures the rate per second.
IOPS measures integer input/output operations per second, while flops measures floating-point arithmetic operations per second.
Clock speed measures cycles per second, while flops measures how many arithmetic operations the hardware can actually perform each second.

examples.everyday: My new graphics card is rated at about ten teraflops, so games run smoothly.
examples.professional: Our training run needs roughly two exaflops of sustained compute, so we're renting a cluster for the week.
examples.analytical: Peak FLOPS measures theoretical throughput, which real workloads rarely reach because memory bandwidth often limits performance.

nuance.analogy: Like a car's top speed on an empty highway: an upper limit that you rarely hit in real traffic.
nuance.etymology: From 'floating-point operation' (flop), with 'per second' added to form the rate, which is usually written in capitals as FLOPS.
common_mistakes: Using 'flops' for a single operation, when the singular 'flop' counts one operation.
Spelling it out as F-L-O-P-S, when Americans say it as one word.

conversation.text: Training FLOPs for a dense transformer are roughly six times the parameter count times the number of tokens.
Do you mean FLOPs as total operations or FLOP/s as throughput? The paper mixes them up.

senses.definition: The act of formalizing something.

core.definition: The process of making something precise by stating it in explicit rules, symbols, or a formal system.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on ZAY, not on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is usually a positive step in logic or mathematics, but it can sound rigid in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formalization mostly in logic, mathematics, computer science, and philosophy, as in 'formalization of the proof.' In casual talk they would say 'making it official' or 'writing it down.' It is used in both academic and business writing, but rarely in conversation.

distinctions.note: Formalization means turning something into an exact symbolic system, while formulation means stating an idea clearly in words.
Standardization makes things match a common norm, whereas formalization makes them explicit and rule-based.

examples.everyday: My brother is into math, so he's always talking about the formalization of his ideas.
examples.professional: The team's next step is the formalization of the API contract so the tests can check it automatically.
examples.analytical: Frege's project of formalization aimed to reduce mathematical reasoning to explicit logical rules.

nuance.analogy: Formalization is like translating a recipe from a cook's memory into a precise ingredient list that a machine can follow exactly.
nuance.etymology: From formalize, from Late Latin formalis, relating to form.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on FOR instead of ZAY.
Using it for everyday paperwork; 'formalization' sounds too technical there.

senses.definition: Given to troublemaking.
Irritable; argumentative; quarrelsome.

core.definition: Irritable, argumentative, or quarrelsome; likely to cause trouble or disagreement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FRAK. The 'ti' is pronounced 'sh,' and the ending is a short, unstressed 'us,' so say 'FRAK-shus.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; describes someone difficult, cranky, or quarrelsome.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fractious in formal writing, politics, and commentary to describe groups or individuals who are hard to manage. In casual talk people usually say 'cranky,' 'argumentative,' or 'difficult.' It often describes a meeting, a party, or a legislature that cannot agree.

distinctions.note: Fractional concerns fractions or small parts; fractious concerns quarrelsome behavior, and the two words are not related in meaning.
Cranky is informal and about a bad mood; fractious is more formal and describes a tendency to quarrel.

examples.everyday: The kids got fractious after the long car ride, so we stopped at a park to let them run.
examples.professional: The project team became fractious after the scope change, and the manager scheduled a short reset meeting.
examples.analytical: The fractious debate among the early church councils shows how doctrinal disputes can divide a community deeply.

nuance.analogy: A fractious group is like a pot of water near boiling, with small bubbles of conflict constantly rising.
nuance.etymology: From fraction (a breaking) plus the suffix -ous, meaning broken or unruly.
common_mistakes: Confusing fractious with fractional because they look alike.
Pronouncing the middle 'ti' as 't' rather than 'sh.'

senses.definition: An instance of breaking, a place where something has broken.
A break in bone or cartilage.
A fault or crack in a rock.
To break, or cause something to break.
To amuse (a person) greatly; to split someone's sides.

core.definition: A break in a bone or cartilage, or a crack or split in something hard, such as a rock or a window.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'ture' ending sounds like 'cher' in American speech, with a 'ch' sound, not 'chur' or 'tur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes damage objectively, and is used with medical or physical contexts more than emotional ones.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fracture' mostly for bones in medical talk, and 'broken bone' or 'break' in everyday speech. A doctor might say 'a hairline fracture' or 'a compound fracture' (where the bone pokes through the skin). In casual talk, 'I broke my arm' is more natural than 'I fractured my arm,' though both are understood.

distinctions.note: 'Break' is the everyday, general word; 'fracture' is more precise and technical, usually for bones or hard materials.
A crack is a narrow line or split that may not separate the pieces; a fracture is a break that may be a more serious separation.
'Rupture' suggests a bursting or tearing, often of soft tissue or a membrane, while a fracture is a break in something rigid.

examples.everyday: I slipped on the ice and got a small fracture in my wrist.
examples.professional: The safety report flagged a fracture in the pressure valve that caused the leak.
examples.analytical: Her argument exposed a fracture in the foundation of the theory, where two incompatible assumptions met.

nuance.analogy: A fracture is like a glass dropped on a tile floor: the pieces are still close, but the structure is no longer whole.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fractura, from frangere, 'to break.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'fracture' for any small break; in everyday talk 'break' is more common for things like a broken toy.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'frack-TURE'.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture speaks of bones being broken, most notably the Passover lamb, whose bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46, RSV). John 19:36 applies this rule to Jesus at his crucifixion, when the soldiers did not break his legs. The Hebrew word behind 'break' here is shavar, meaning to break or shatter.

fracture.etymology: From Middle English *fracture*, from Old French *fracture*, from Latin *frāctūra* (“a breach, fracture, cleft”), from *frango* (“to break”), past participle *frāctus*, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **bʰreg-*, whence also English *break*.

senses.definition: In a state of panic, worry, frenzy, or rush.
senses.example: They returned the missing child to his frantic mother.

senses.definition: Extremely energetic.
senses.example: frantic music

core.definition: Wildly anxious, hurried, or out of control, as if in a panic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second vowel is a short, quick i, so the word has two clear syllables and the final k is hard.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests stress, panic, or loss of control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frantic for people who are panicking or very rushed, such as a parent looking for a lost child or a shopper before a holiday. It is common in everyday speech and writing. It can also be used lightly for very busy periods, such as frantic week at work.

distinctions.note: Hectic describes a busy, chaotic schedule or day; frantic describes the emotional state of the people in it, usually with panic.
Frenzied is more intense and suggests wild, uncontrolled activity; frantic is common and often used about worry or urgency.

examples.everyday: I was frantic when I could not find my keys, and then I realized they were in the fridge.
examples.professional: The team was frantic on Friday trying to fix the failed deployment before the Monday client demo.
examples.analytical: The author describes the frantic pace of modern life as a symptom of a deeper anxiety about meaning and control.

nuance.analogy: Frantic is like a kettle boiling over: the energy is there, but it has no direction and makes a mess.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English frenetik, from Old French frenetique, from Latin phreneticus, from Greek phrenitis, inflammation of the brain or delirium.
common_mistakes: Using frantic for an energetic but happy person, when lively or energetic is more natural.
Saying fran-TICK with stress on the second syllable.

frantic.etymology: From Middle English *frantike*, *frentik*, variant of *frenetik*, from Old French *frenetique*, from Late Latin *phreneticus*, alteration of *phreniticus*, from *φρενιτικός* (“mad, suffering from inflammation of the brain”), from *φρενῖτις* (“inflammation…

senses.definition: In a state of hurry, panic or wild activity.
senses.example: Preparations for the president's arrival made for a frenzied week.

core.definition: In a state of wild hurry, panic, or intense activity that seems out of control.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FREN. The final -ied is pronounced as a single syllable, like 'eed', not as two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests a loss of control, panic, or chaotic energy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frenzied for crowds, last-minute work, shopping, or chaotic moments, often in news and everyday talk. It sounds vivid but not extreme, so it works in both conversation and writing. People say 'a frenzied rush' or 'a frenzied search' naturally.

distinctions.note: Frenetic stresses fast, restless energy, while frenzied stresses wild loss of control or panic.
Frantic describes desperate worry, while frenzied describes a whirl of activity, often with a crowd.

examples.everyday: The stores were packed with frenzied shoppers the day before Thanksgiving.
examples.professional: After the server failed, the operations team made frenzied calls to restore service before customers noticed.
examples.analytical: Historians often describe the frenzied politics of that decade as a reaction to deep economic fear.

nuance.analogy: A frenzied crowd is like a swarm of bees disturbed from a hive, moving fast and everywhere at once.
nuance.etymology: From frenzy, from Old French frenesie, from Late Latin phrenesis, from Greek phrenesis, a derangement of the mind.
common_mistakes: Using frenzied as a noun; it is an adjective, so say 'a frenzied rush', not 'a frenzied'.
Saying 'frenzied' with a stress on the second syllable; stress FREN.

senses.definition: A category homomorphism; a morphism from a source category to a target category which maps objects to objects and arrows to arrows (either covariantly or contravariantly), in such a way as to preserve morphism composition and identities.
senses.example: In the category of categories 𝐂𝐚𝐭 the objects are categories and the morphisms are functors.

senses.definition: A function word.
A function object.
A structure allowing a function to apply within a generic type, in a way that is conceptually similar to a functor in category theory.

core.definition: In mathematics, especially category theory, a map between categories that sends objects to objects and arrows to arrows while preserving composition and identities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FUNK. The final r is pronounced clearly, and the vowel in the last syllable is the open American sound in 'door', not a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and computer scientists use functor in category theory, and functional programmers use it in discussions of Haskell's type classes. Outside those fields, the word is rare. Do not confuse it with function; a functor is a structure-preserving mapping between categories, not simply a function between sets.

distinctions.note: A function maps elements of one set to another, while a functor maps whole categories and their structure.
A morphism is an arrow between objects in a category, while a functor is a map between categories that preserves morphisms.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies math told me a functor is basically a way of translating one structure into another.
examples.professional: In the Haskell codebase, the list type implements the Functor class, so we can map over it cleanly.
examples.analytical: A covariant functor preserves the direction of morphisms, so it must send composable arrows to composable arrows while respecting identities.

nuance.analogy: A functor is like a translator who converts an entire book from one language to another, keeping the grammar and meaning of every sentence intact.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 20th century from function, on the model of Latin functor, one who performs.
common_mistakes: Treating functor as the same as function, which misses the structure-preserving requirement.
Using functor in everyday English for a person who performs a function; that sense is rare and dated.

core.definition: A respected Pharisee and teacher of the law in Jerusalem, who counseled the Jewish council to leave the apostles alone and taught Paul.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MAY. The final two syllables are weak, so say 'lee-uhl' rather than 'lee-ell'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; in Christian contexts he is seen as a wise and fair-minded teacher.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches and Bible classes, Gamaliel is mostly a name from the New Testament. People might say 'Gamaliel' when discussing Acts or Paul's education. The name is also used for people in general, but it is uncommon outside religious settings.

distinctions.note: Rabban Gamaliel the Elder is the grandfather of Gamaliel of Acts and was also a Pharisee; the two should not be confused.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group talked about Gamaliel today, since he's the calm voice in Acts who tells the council to wait and see.
examples.professional: In my sermon on Acts 5, I used Gamaliel as an example of a leader who weighs evidence before acting against a movement.
examples.analytical: Gamaliel's counsel in Acts 5:34-39 is read as a test of divine origin, where a movement that lasts is judged to be from God.

nuance.analogy: Gamaliel is like the experienced senior colleague who advises a committee to wait before acting on a rumor.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Gamliel, meaning God is my reward.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as GAM-uh-LEE-el; the stress falls on MAY.
Confusing Gamaliel the Pharisee in Acts with Rabban Gamaliel the Elder, his grandfather.
nuance.biblical_note: Gamaliel (Greek Gamaliēl, from Hebrew Gamliel, 'God is my reward') is a Pharisee and respected teacher of the law. In Acts 5:34-39 he advises the Sanhedrin to leave the apostles alone, arguing that if their work is of human origin it will fail, but if it is of God it cannot be overthrown. In Acts 22:3 Paul says he was brought up at Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel and trained in the strict manner of the law. Numbers 1:10 also names a different Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur, a leader of the tribe of Manasseh.

senses.definition: A cut of quick-cured pork leg.
A victory in backgammon achieved when the opponent has not borne off a single stone.
A rope fastening a bowsprit to the stem of a ship (usually called a gammoning).
(rare) Backgammon (the game itself).
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (dated) Chatter, ridiculous nonsense.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To cure bacon by salting.
To beat by a gammon (without the opponent bearing off a stone).
To lash with ropes (on a ship).
(dated) To deceive; to lie plausibly to.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A cut of cured pork leg, usually sliced and served as ham in a meal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the second to a soft un sound. Many learners add a full o vowel or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a food term, and in American English it is rare and mainly found in British or historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, Americans usually say ham or cured pork for this cut, so gammon is uncommon in American menus and shopping. You may see it in British cookbooks or in food writing about British pubs. If you want the American word, ask for ham or smoked ham.

distinctions.note: Ham is the common American word for a cured pork leg; gammon is mainly a British term for the same type of cut, often sold raw and cured.
Bacon comes from the pork belly or back, while gammon comes from the hind leg, so the two cuts differ in shape and texture.

examples.everyday: At the grocery store, I asked for a smoked ham steak instead of gammon, because the clerk did not know what I meant.
examples.professional: The supplier listed the product as gammon, but our American customers expect a product labeled ham.
examples.analytical: Culinary terms such as gammon reveal how regional vocabulary can separate British and American food cultures even when the product is nearly identical.

nuance.analogy: Gammon is like a British name for the same cut that Americans call ham, similar to how Americans say cookie where the British say biscuit.
nuance.etymology: From Old French gambon, meaning a ham or leg of meat, related to gamb, meaning leg.
common_mistakes: Using gammon in an American grocery store, where clerks may not recognize it.
Stressing the second syllable as ga-MON.
Confusing gammon with the board game backgammon.

gammon.etymology: From Middle English **gammon*, *gambon*, from Old French *gambon*, from *gambe* (“leg”), from Late Latin *gamba*, from Ancient Greek *καμπή*.

senses.definition: Very showy or ornamented, now especially when excessive, or in a tasteless or vulgar manner.
senses.example: They were all trapped out in the gaudiest of clothes.

senses.definition: Fun; merry; festive.
A reunion held by one of the colleges of the University of Oxford for alumni, normally during the long vacation.

core.definition: Very bright, showy, or decorated in a tasteless way, with more ornament than seems appropriate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GAW, and the ending is a simple ee. The vowel is the open aw sound of caught, not the o of go.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes something as tasteless or excessive, though it can sound more playful in a casual context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gaudy for jewelry, décor, clothing, or cars that look too flashy. It is an informal, expressive word and is not usually used for polite compliments. A neutral alternative is bold, while flashy is a good choice in most conversations.

distinctions.note: Flashy describes eye-catching style and can be positive, while gaudy is a criticism of tastelessness.
Ornate describes elaborate decoration that may be admired, while gaudy suggests it is excessive and cheap.

examples.everyday: That gold lamp in the living room is a little gaudy, honestly, but my aunt loves it.
examples.professional: The client rejected the gaudy color scheme and asked for something more understated.
examples.analytical: Critics often treated gaudy display as evidence of social insecurity rather than simple taste.

nuance.analogy: A gaudy outfit is like a neon sign in a quiet library: it is hard to ignore and out of place.
nuance.etymology: Probably from gaud, an ornament or trinket, with uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel like go instead of caught.
Using gaudy as a compliment; it usually criticizes.

gaudy.etymology: From Middle English *gaudi*, from Old French *gaudie*, from Medieval Latin *gaudia*.

senses.definition: To take a break from one's present circumstances; to journey (to), especially on holiday.
senses.example: This place is really getting me down. I need to get away for a while.

senses.definition: To avoid capture; to escape; to flee (from).
senses.example: Surround the bank! Don't let the robber get away!

senses.definition: To move away (from).
senses.example: Get away from the edge of the cliff!

senses.definition: To start moving; to depart.
senses.example: The train got away exactly on time.

senses.definition: To slip from one's control.
senses.example: I can't cope any more. Things are getting away from me.

senses.definition: Expressing disbelief.
senses.example: You bought that for twenty pounds? Get away!

core.definition: To leave your normal routine for a short break, often by going on a trip.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'way', and the 'a' is reduced, so it sounds like 'guh-tuh-WAY'. In speech the t links into the following vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive and refreshing when used for a break; neutral when used for escaping.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'get away' for taking a short vacation or break: 'We need to get away this weekend.' It also means escaping from someone or something. As an interjection, 'Get away!' or 'Get out!' means 'No way!' when you doubt a claim. A natural reply to a plan is 'Where are you going?'

distinctions.note: Take a vacation is more general and planned, while get away suggests briefly escaping ordinary pressures, often for just a weekend.
Escape stresses an urgent or forced leaving from danger or confinement; get away can be relaxed or deliberate.

examples.everyday: We need to get away for a few days before the holidays.
